summary: CCC-built 1933 L-4 lookout in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, no longer staffed, saved from a 2012 removal order by a 2014 act of Congress.

facts.design: L-4 style, 14 by 14 ft wood-frame ground house with exterior catwalk and cable anchor system
facts.status_note: Not used for fire detection since the 1980s; restored and maintained by Friends of Green Mountain volunteers.

access.note: Located in the Glacier Peak Wilderness; reaching it requires a wilderness trail hike, not a drive.

visit.trail_note: Summit of Green Mountain, Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, about 17 miles east of Darrington per a lookout fan site.

events.note: Built by the Civilian Conservation Corps to a standard Forest Service L-4 design.
Roof replaced and walls, windows and doors repaired after heavy snowfall damage.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on February 22, 1988 (per Wikipedia infobox).
Added to the National Historic Lookout Register October 28, 1991.
Closed to the public in the mid-1990s due to a damaged foundation and catwalk.
Building dismantled piece by piece after its new foundation was damaged by snowfall; pieces flown out by helicopter for repair.
Foundation repaired and the lookout reconstructed on site, with pieces helicoptered back up after road-washout delays in 2003 and 2006.
Federal court in Seattle sided with Wilderness Watch's lawsuit and ordered the structure removed.
Green Mountain Lookout Heritage Protection Act passed by Congress and signed by President Obama, blocking removal.

evidence.supports: 1933 CCC build to standard design with catwalk and cable anchor
evidence.quote: The single-story wood-frame structure measures 14 by 14 feet (4.3 by 4.3 m) and was built according to a standard National Forest Service design in 1933 by the Civilian Conservation Corps.
In 1950, the roof was replaced and walls, windows, and doors were repaired after heavy snowfall damaged the building the previous winter.

in the mid-1990s, the building was closed to the public due to a damaged foundation and catwalk. In 2002, after a newly installed foundation was severely damaged by snowfall, the building was dismantled piece by piece, with pieces flown by helicopter to be repaired off-site.

After delays from road washouts in 2003 and 2006, the foundation was repaired in 2009 and the building was reconstructed shortly thereafter, with the pieces flown back up to the mountaintop via helicopter.

evidence.supports: 2012 court order and 2014 Act of Congress
evidence.quote: In 2012, a federal court in Seattle sided with the group and ordered the removal of the structure... The act was passed by Congress and signed into law by President Obama in 2014, superseding the court order.

evidence.supports: L-4 design and Friends of Green Mountain restoration
evidence.quote: The structure, a classic L-4, 14- by 14-ft ground house once common in the Pacific Northwest, has been lovingly restored by the Friends of Green Mountain.

notes_for_editor: Brief lists NRHP added date as implied by 1988-numbered reference (88000117); Wikipedia infobox gives exact date Feb 22, 1988, which resolves the record. Access is wilderness hike-in, not drive-up; no mileage figure verified beyond a secondary fan site's '17 miles east of Darrington' claim, which was not cited as fact in the story.
